## Introduction ### Overview Since [week 12](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#quarto-documents), you've been writing your R code in Quarto documents, using a basic YAML header, code chunks, and Markdown text. In this session, we'll take a closer look at each of these components, and at what happens when you render a document. ### Learning goals In this session, you will learn: - What happens when Quarto renders a document - More about **YAML** syntax and useful options in the YAML header - How to use **chunk options**, and how to set them for a whole document - How to label chunks and include R output in your Markdown text - How to use the visual editor for Quarto documents - How to render a document to Markdown that displays well on GitHub ## Setting up Create a new folder `week14`, and in it, create a new Quarto document `week14a.qmd` ([Creating a Quarto document](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#creating-a-quarto-document)). ## How rendering works When you render a Quarto document, two programs do the work: 1. **knitr** runs all code chunks, in a new R session, and creates a plain Markdown file with your text, code, and the code's output. 2. **Pandoc** converts that Markdown file to the final output format. This two-step process means that the same `.qmd` file can be rendered to many output formats, like HTML, PDF, Word, and even slide decks and websites^[ This website and its slides were made with Quarto, too!], and that Quarto isn't limited to R: it can also run code in other languages like Python. Quarto is the next-generation version of R Markdown, in case you have heard of that. ### Rendering from the terminal You can also render a Quarto document from the terminal, using the `quarto render` command: ```bash quarto render week14/week14a.qmd ``` This does a **one-time render**: just like `Preview`, it runs all code in a new R session and creates `week14a.html` next to `week14a.qmd`. But unlike `Preview`, it does not show the result in the Viewer pane. To look at the output, open the HTML file yourself. So, `Preview` is handy while you are writing and editing a document, whereas `quarto render` is handy to simply produce the final output file. ## Components of Quarto documents As you saw in week 12, a Quarto document has three main components: the YAML header, code chunks, and Markdown text. We'll take a closer look at each of these now. ### YAML header The YAML header contains settings for the document: metadata like the title and author, and options for the output format. Recall from week 12 that each line contains a `key: value` pair (with a space after the colon). Here is an example with a few more options: ```yaml --- title: "Week 14: Quarto" subtitle: "Beyond the basics" author: "Jane Doe" date: 2026-11-23 format: html: embed-resources: true toc: true theme: cosmo --- ``` - Keys can be nested by indenting them with two spaces: above, `html` is nested under `format`, and `embed-resources`, `toc`, and `theme` are options for the `html` output format. - `embed-resources: true` makes Quarto put everything, including any figures, into a single HTML file, so you can download that one file from OSC and open or share it. - `toc: true` adds a table of contents. - `theme` picks one of Quarto's [25 built-in themes](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html), which change the fonts, colors, etc. - There are many more [options for HTML output](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html). ::: callout-tip #### Project-level YAML You can also set YAML options for all Quarto documents in a project in a file called `_quarto.yml` in the project's root directory (see the [Quarto docs on projects](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/project-configuration.html)). Options in a document's own YAML header override these. ::: #### YAML lists Some keys take a list of values, which can be written in two ways: ```yaml # Block syntax: each item on a new line, preceded by a dash and a space author: - Jane Doe - John Smith # Inline syntax: comma-separated values inside square brackets keywords: [RNA-seq, mosquito, Plasmodium] ``` #### Quotes and comments In YAML, strings usually don't need quotes, but they do when they contain special characters like `:` or `#`. For example, the title in the example above, `"Week 14: Quarto"`, needs quotes because of the colon. To be safe, you can always quote strings. As in R and the shell, a `#` starts a comment. ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: YAML header 1. Change the YAML header of your `week14a.qmd` to include a title, a subtitle, two authors (you and a classmate) in block syntax, today's date, a table of contents, and the `darkly` theme. Render the document. 2. **Predict** what will happen in each of the following cases, then try them one by one (and undo each change afterwards): - You remove the space after the colon in `toc: true`. - You remove the quotes around a title that contains a colon. ::: ### Code chunks ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} #### Showing the output below each chunk _(Click to expand)_ Positron can optionally show the output of each chunk right below it in the editor, as RStudio does by default. To turn this on, open the Settings and enable `quarto.inlineOutput.enabled`. With this setting turned on, Positron runs the code of each Quarto document in a separate R session, whose working directory is the document's folder, and whose Console is not shown by default (to show it, enable `console.showNotebookConsoles`). Because you use `here()` for file paths ([week 13](../week13/w13a_data-wrangling.qmd#file-paths-in-quarto-documents)), your code works the same either way. ::: #### Chunk options You can change how a chunk behaves with **chunk options**: lines at the top of a chunk that start with `#|`, where each `#|` line sets one option. For example, this chunk would be shown in the rendered document, but not run: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: false install.packages("tidyverse") ``` ```` ::: A few useful chunk options: - `#| eval: false` --- Show the code but don't run it. - `#| echo: false` --- Run the code and show its output, but hide the code itself. This is useful if you want to show a figure but not the code used to create it. - `#| include: false` --- Run the code, but show neither the code nor its output. - `#| warning: false` and `#| message: false` --- Hide warnings and messages, such as the ones printed when loading some packages. - `#| fig-cap: "Your figure caption"` --- Add a figure caption. - `#| fig-show: hide` --- Hide figures. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} Install packages in the console rather than in a chunk. Otherwise, they will be installed again every time you render the document. ::: Chunk options can also be written inside the curly braces, as in ```` ```{r, echo=FALSE} ````, but the `#|` syntax is preferred. More chunk options can be found [here](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html). ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r eval=TRUE}} # Example code chunk 2 * 2 ``` ```` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| eval: true 2 * 3 ``` ```` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 6 ``` ::: ::: #### Global vs. chunk-specific options If the default code chunk settings don’t fit your needs, you can change them for the whole document in the YAML section under `execute:`. For example, if you don’t want to show your R code to your readers, you can set `echo: false` which hides all code by default. If you later want to show the code for a specific chunk, you can turn it back on just for that chunk using `echo: true`. For example: ```yaml --- title: "My report" format: html: embed-resources: true execute: echo: false warning: false --- ``` Note that `execute:` is a top-level key, not nested under `format:`. #### Chunk labels You can give a chunk a **label** with `#| label: `. Labels must be unique within a document and cannot contain spaces. They show up in messages during rendering, which makes it easier to find the chunk that caused a problem: ::: {.cell} ````{.cell-code} ```{{r}} #| label: my-first-chunk 2 + 3 ``` ```` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: #### Running all chunks above Besides `Run Cell`, which runs the current chunk, the line above each chunk has a `Run Above` button, which runs all code chunks _above_ the current chunk. This is useful when you've restarted R or opened a document in a new session, and want to get back to where you were. ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: Chunk options and self-contained documents Add code chunks to your document to do the following: 1. Load the _tidyverse_, using a chunk option to hide its messages. 2. Check the number of rows and columns of the `diamonds` data set (which comes with _ggplot2_). Then, select its first 5 columns, keep only rows with a carat greater than 0.23, and rename the `color` variable to `colors`. 3. Create a scatter plot with `carat` on the x-axis and `depth` on the y-axis. 4. Temporarily **remove** `embed-resources: true` from your YAML header and render. In the Explorer, what was created besides the HTML file? Download only the HTML file and open it on your computer: what's missing, and why? Then put `embed-resources: true` back. ::: ### Markdown text The "default text" in Quarto documents is Markdown, unlike in R scripts, where everything is considered code until commented out by `#`. Quarto text syntax is based on Pandoc Markdown which is similar to the original Markdown syntax we discussed in [week 2](../week02/w2d_markdown.qmd). #### Inline code You can include the output of R code directly in your Markdown text with **inline code**: a backtick, the letter `r` and a space, your code, and a closing backtick. For example, this text: ```markdown The iris data set contains `r nrow(iris)` flowers. ``` Renders as: > The iris data set contains 150 flowers. This way, numbers in your text are computed when you render the document, so they always match your data and code --- no more copy-pasting numbers. ::: exercise #### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: Inline code 1. Add a sentence to your document that reports the number of rows of the `diamonds` data set with inline code, and render.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ For example: The diamonds data set has `r nrow(diamonds)` rows.
2. **Predict**: what will the rendered document show if you leave out the `r` and the space, i.e. `` `nrow(diamonds)` ``? Render to check.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ Without the `r`, it is regular Markdown inline code formatting: the text `nrow(diamonds)` is shown in a code font, and the code is not run.
::: ## Source editor vs. Visual editor So far, you've edited Quarto documents in the default **source editor**, where you type everything yourself: the text, the code chunks, and the YAML header. This gives you full control, but requires knowing some Markdown and Quarto syntax. Positron also has a **visual editor** for Quarto documents, which is the same one you may have used for Markdown files in VS Code in [week 7](../week07/w7b_scripts2.qmd#markdown-setup), since both use the Quarto extension. In the visual editor, you can format text and add elements like tables and images with toolbar buttons, and see roughly how your document will look as you write, much like in Word or Google Docs. To switch between the two editors, click the `...` button in the top-right of the editor, and select "**Edit in Visual Mode**" or "**Edit in Source Mode**". ## Output for GitHub GitHub shows HTML files as raw code, not as web pages. To share a rendered document in a GitHub repository, like for your final project, you can _also_ render it to GitHub-Flavored Markdown (`gfm`), which GitHub displays nicely: ```yaml format: html: embed-resources: true gfm: default ``` With two formats, the `Preview` button only renders the first one. To render both formats, use `quarto render` in the terminal ([Rendering from the terminal](#rendering-from-the-terminal)). This creates a `.md` file, plus a `_files` folder with the figures: commit both to your repository. ## Before next week: install packages for week 15 Installing the R packages for next week's RNA-seq analysis can take 10--20 minutes, so let's get that started now. Run the following code in the R console --- we'll go over what these commands do next week: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("BiocManager") install.packages("pheatmap") BiocManager::install(c("DESeq2", "EnhancedVolcano")) ``` ::: If the installation doesn't finish before the end of class, or you weren't able to start it, please make sure to run it before next week's class (see the [week 15 overview](../week15/w15_overview.qmd#before-class-install-packages)).
